utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, the Defence is ready to bring the accused, Miroslav Tadic, to testify. So I would please ask him to come to the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. One of the judges isn't getting the English translation in spite of being on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the translation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution can hear clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the translation now. Can you hear? One two three, one two three. Can you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The two of us can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the translation now, one two three, one two three. Can you hear, one two three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can hear. Mr. Lukic, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tadic. Could you please tell us your first and last name, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us, do you have any nicknames?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, my nickname is Brko. And all of my family is also called that, my wife is called Mrs. Brko and my son is called Brkos.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we have a lot of information about you on record through conversations with you, with the Prosecutor, I would like to cover that in a different way, not all that is already known through your statements and also from the indictment, but before we move to this information, could you please tell the Chamber why you decided to testify? The first thing that I want to ask you is when did you hear about the indictment issued against you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Before I begin my answer, I would like to just say a couple of sentences about today. Five days ago -- five years ago, on the 14th of February, 1998, I surrendered to SFOR. This was at the same place where the major exchange took place in 1991 that is discussed here. Regarding the indictment, I found out about it some time in 1995, in late 1995 or early 1996 from the media, newspapers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I think there is a mistake on second page, line 23, when the major exchange took place in 1991, shouldn't it be 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, in 1991, there was already talk about this exchange here and we will talk some more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the exchanges between Yugoslavia and Croatia in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are precisely the exchanges that I am talking about and this is where I surrendered in the same place where these exchanges were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you have your first contacts with investigators from the Prosecutor's office and how did you get in touch with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My first contacts with the investigators began in the spring of 1996. The people from the Croatian side with whom I cooperated and worked, so from them, I found out that investigators were interested in me and that they were willing, if I was willing, to conduct several interviews with me by telephone. They even left me a telephone number that I should call.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the people that you cooperated with, are you thinking of the people who worked on the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, the people who worked on the Croatian side because the investigators were in Orasje which belongs to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you got this telephone number, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I thought for a couple of days, I thought about what to do for about ten days, perhaps. I didn't want to consult with anyone, not even to my nearest and dearest ones. I didn't tell them anything about it and then one day, I think that it was the 26th of April, 1996, I called The Hague. A woman was on the other end, an interpreter, and she said that the person that I was looking for was not there, that was Marija Velikonja and she said that I should leave my telephone number and she would call me when she comes back in about ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long this first telephone conversation lasted between you and the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: This first telephone conversation lasted about two hours, from two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at the end of that conversation, did you agree on anything?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, we did agree. First of all, I had to do an identification in a certain way, and then we agreed that she would call me again in a day or so and she asked me if I could send her any of the documents that we mentioned. I told her that that was not a problem, that I would send them by fax, she gave me a fax number and that's when the conversation ended. After a couple of days, I used a fax in an institution to send to send about 60 documents to Ms. Velikonja and after a couple of days, perhaps, she called me again. This second conversation was mainly clarification of the documents that I had sent her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did this second conversation last?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The same, about two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when did you decide to voluntarily surrender to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's interesting to say that I had another conversation, I think that that was the third conversation, and she told me then that she will not talk to me anymore and she asked if she could speak with my lawyer and if she could see my lawyer because she would come, I think she said in the month of June in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1996, June 1996 that she could come to Orasje and that's how it was. My lawyer went to Orasje and they had several meetings, perhaps he stayed for three or four hours there, and then he returned. After that, Ms. Velikonja came to Samac, she didn't have any contacts with me but she did have contacts with the lawyer and after that, we didn't talk again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was when did you decide to surrender and how did this proceed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: These conversations that I had with the Prosecution -- the Prosecutor's office, it was obvious that from the beginning, I was thinking of getting in touch in a certain way and resolving this situation that I found myself in. Finally, in 1997, in late 1997 and early 1998, talks began. I think they were the representatives of the US embassy, we had talks with them. I don't think they were representatives of the Tribunal. So this was finalised in the end in mid-February, on the 13th of February, this was finalised and concluded so that I should surrender to the SFOR on the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 14th of February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, I would just like to say one sentence before this event. These negotiations of mine also included the organs of Republika Srpska and of the local authorities. General Shinseki was also present during the negotiations and he issued instructions to the negotiators. On the 14th of February, around this time, the police of Republika Srpska came and arrested me and I was handed over to the SFOR at 3.00 p.m., around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: After the surrender, we went through the regular routine procedure. I was searched, things that I couldn't take with me were given back, and then I was taken to the base in Tuzla, that's where the SFOR accompanied me. Mr. Milan Simic was with me, General Shinseki was there waiting for us and in a way, he commended us for this act and in a conversation which lasted about an hour, he said that, I don't know, "the procedure would be finished in three to six months," that's what he said, because our condition upon surrender was that this should not take an indeterminate amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there were also before you two accused who had surrendered to this Tribunal; is this right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me when did you give an interview or have an interview with the Prosecution once you came to the Tribunal or were taken to the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: As soon as the Prosecutor's office requested that, and this was in late March, they talked to my lawyer and to myself and they asked us whether we wanted to give this interview and I didn't have anything against that so I think on the 26th of March of that year, 1998, I did agree to be interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor. I think it was either the 26th or the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A part of my question wasn't recorded on page 6, line 20, I asked you: Were you and Milan Simic the first two accused who voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal and you answered yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that we were the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this interview that you gave and which has been tendered as an exhibit here, which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in March 1998, did you give that interview under any pressure or did you agree to it voluntarily of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Just like everything else that happened before that, my conversation with the Prosecutor and my surrender were just something that I had decided to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Allow me to mention that in the negotiations about surrender, the lawyer of Mr. Zaric also took part in -- and he surrendered about ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this was Mr. Pisarevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the authorities of Republika Srpska take part in these negotiations; do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The authorities of Republika Srpska did participate, I don't want to mention them now, and also the local authorities from Samac did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will move to your particulars. Since some of that is already contained in the interview, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to anything, I'm just seeking a clarification. I wonder if Mr. Lukic could clarify, he mentioned, asked the witness, Mr. Tadic, if Republika Srpska officials participated in the negotiations. I wonder if we could be clear about what particular negotiations he is -- Mr. Tadic is talking about. Are they negotiations upon surrender, are they negotiations of the Prosecutors over the telephone or are they some other negotiations because it may assume, it may assume some importance later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I and the witness understood one another but perhaps the question was not well formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which negotiations pertaining to what decisions -- in which negotiations pertaining to what decisions did the Republika Srpska and local authorities participate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I said that the Republika Srpska and local authorities participated in the negotiations upon surrender in February 1998. I didn't mention any names, but if necessary, I can provide some names but I think that this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary. You were born on the 12th of May, 1937 in the village of Novi Grad in the municipality of Odzak where your family is also from and you described in the interview on page 9 and 10, you talked about your schooling, your work history, and experience and this is something that I do not really wish to talk about because this is something that you have stated and this is something that you stand by; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you come to Samac, how long have you been living in Samac, this is mentioned in the interview but I would like to know what you were doing, what your job was in Samac once you came to live there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I went to university and at that time, it was normal for students to get grants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It states here 1991, can you please correct that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No. It should be 1961, that's when I went to university. At that time, it was usual for students to receive grants, scholarships and I got a scholarship from the Samac municipality because also my intention was that once I completed my studies I would come and work in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when was -- when did you come back to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction in the transcript. I don't believe it is very significant but it would be good to have everything clear, the condition of receiving scholarship was to return to Bosanski Samac, this is actually what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, before you continue, I know that you said in your question on page 8 and 9 that you don't want to talk about or questioned Mr. Tadic about his work history and experience; however, I have a recollection from one of the interviews with the OTP, Mr. Tadic, you were a member of the armed forces, I think, and was it that you went to Suez?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I intended to ask, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Perfect. Then, Mr. Lukic, I will leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the intention but I first wanted to deal with personal data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. Do it at the time that you think is correct from the point of view of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since when have you lived in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I've already said that after two years of university, in the autumn of 1963, I came to work in Samac although I am not from Samac originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you work as a teacher in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Starting in 1963 up until the end of 1983 so just above 20 years. That's the time I spent working at the educational centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a teacher, first primary grades and second upper grades of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will say a few more words about your origins, I think that's important for the case. We have asked almost every witness here how long his or her ancestors had lived for in the area and I will ask you the same, for how long have your ancestors lived in the municipality of Odzak and in that area in general?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My village called Novi Grad is not a town at all, it's a village, although the word Grad in Serbian means town and the village has had that name for some 300 years and my ancestors lived there from the very early days. We were there when the Turks arrived and left the area, when Austria came and left we were there to see the communism through and that's how it was. We were also there when this unfortunate war came in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the interview you gave to OTP on page 14, you said that you didn't have parents, can you explain briefly what happened to your parents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I have already explained that in the interview and I wouldn't like to go back into that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many siblings do you have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I have two brothers and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who is the eldest?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I am the eldest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, please, were you war orphans?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, not just myself, but the rest of us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell me, before the events of 1991 and 1992, did you have any relatives living in the village Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Most of my relatives live in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And have done so --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, have done so throughout all of these years since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me about your wife?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My wife's name is Mirjana.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where does her family hail from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: From my village as well, Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your interview with OTP, you've described your family situation however there have been some changes since so could we please clarify, how many children do you have, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Let me just mention that my wife is a war orphan as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I presume we will get some clarity, I think we all know war orphans means World War II but for the record, that we know it's World War II, and maybe we should have some sense as to who the alleged perpetrators were, was it Germany, was it Croatia, was it somebody else? I leave it up to you to handle the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very difficult for me to get this story out of my client. I've tried over the past three years. I've asked him whether he wanted to tell this story he said no, so I wouldn't insist, but however, if you wish I can ask him again and see whether he would like to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I don't want to upset you by asking this so I would ask for just a very brief answer but it would give us some sense as to who the -- which side were the alleged perpetrators of these deaths so just, you know, in one sentence or two, not anything long. I don't want to upset you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to leave that for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll come back to it later. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've asked you about your children.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I said -- or rather you've already mentioned that I have a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war and after the war, did your son get married, does he have children now, where does he live now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My son got married during the war. He has lived with me throughout the entire time. He's living with me now and he has two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your daughter, where was she during the war, is she married, does she have children?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My daughter got married in 1987 and has lived in Switzerland since, she has two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the ethnicity of your son-in-law, your daughter's husband?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: He is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you religious?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now return to what Judge Williams mentioned. We know when you served in the army, it is stated in the interview but can you it will us in what branch of service did you serve and was there anything peculiar about your military service?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I went to serve in the army in 1957. I served in Karlovac in Croatia and I was in the engineering corps. After the initial three months of training, I was transferred to Pozarevac which is in Serbia and sometime in late 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: -- no, in 1958, in late 1958, there were amongst 350 soldiers who went from Yugoslavia to Egypt, I was among them. I went to Egypt on the 4th of December, 1958 and I remained there for six and a half months approximately. So that means that I returned sometime in mid-June 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within what forces were you serving and under whose flag were you serving in Egypt?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Those were the UN forces. At the time, there were ten states providing their troops for the UN forces, Yugoslavia was among them, Brazil, India, Sweden, Norway, Canada --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a photograph which had been analysed during the OTP interview and in order to avoid any confusion, I would like the photograph to be shown to the witness and tendered into evidence just so that we avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, what is depicted in this picture, is that the photograph that you had shown to the OTP investigators during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the photographs. There were a number of photographs shown during the interview and I can't recollect whether this particular one was shown as well. This was taken, I believe, in spring of 1988, I apologise, spring of 1989 [As interpreted]. It was taken in Suez. We went to greet Tito as he was arriving in Egypt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were you -- where are you in this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well I'm here, 40 some years ago. These are two Egyptian soldiers, this is a non-commissioned officer of the Yugoslav army and this here are just citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please record that Miroslav Tadic indicated the second person from the right as himself in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And we can also get a clarification for the transcript because it says on 25 that this photograph was the spring of 1989. It's obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what year was this? Please take a minute and think about it and tell us when was the picture taken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I might have made a mistake. I said that it was in the spring of 1959 when this photograph was taken, springtime, January, February, or March, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this photograph be admitted into evidence, please, if there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have a moustache here and this is what you told to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph will be admitted and the -- Mr. Tadic as shown as described by counsel. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the number is D143/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions regarding your past. Were you ever, and if so how long, a member of any party in the pre-war Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: While I was in Egypt, I was given a recommendation to become a member of the then League of Communists of Yugoslavia. The recommendation followed me to Odzak through the usual channels; however, I didn't go back to Odzak immediately after finishing my service. It wasn't until 1961 that I came to Odzak and the recommendation was already there waiting and this is when I was admitted into the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain as a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists up until 1972, approximately around that time. At the time, I worked in a school as you already know, and I usually worked in the afternoon shift. The organisation of the League of Communists was then made based on neighborhoods where people lived and the meetings were usually held in the afternoon, therefore, I very seldom was able to attend them. The then secretary exerted pressure on me asking -- requesting that I attend meetings. I said that I couldn't, and then he said that I would be removed from the records and in 1972, that's exactly what he told me, that I was removed from the records due to inactivity. That doesn't mean that I was discharged from the party or anything like that, I was simply removed from the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that have any impact on your career, on your life in Samac then, what was life like for those who were not members of the party but still had some public roles?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Since I didn't really have a political career, I had no political ambitions, it basically had no impact. I continued with my job. I had some minor problems but nothing significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of some other political party after leaving the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and what about nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was no other political party and I did not join any political party when the multi-party elections were held either. I am not a member of any political party now either. I might become a member of some party after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So to conclude, after leaving the League of Communists, you never joined another political party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any convictions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No. I've never even been a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to move to a different topic. I would like to ask you a few questions regarding your acquaintance with the other accused from this case. You also talked about that in your interview, but we would like to hear some details on that topic. Before the war, did you personally know Dr. Blagoje Simic, and when I say before the war, I would like to be specific, before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I said that during my interview and I'm saying it now, I did not know Mr. Blagoje Simic. I said that I knew his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I got to know Simo Zaric as a student. At the school where I worked, he was one of the students; however, later when he finished school, he went on his way, went to university, and then on his return to Samac, we didn't have any contacts or any common interests. More intensive contacts between us actually began once he retired and this was in the late 1980s, in the late 1990s, in 1989. He would come to my cafe, we would play billiards and so on, we would socialise, but before that, we didn't really know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before the war, did you know Milan Simic, did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, before the war, I didn't know Milan Simic but I knew his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you know Stevan Todorovic before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him. He stated here in the courtroom that he was one of my students, but I don't remember him as a student. It was probably -- he was probably an average student because a person usually remembers the best and the worst students so I don't remember him. Afterwards when he went away to university, he spent along time with his studies and when he returned to Samac, we didn't have any common interests. I didn't know him. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you visit Simo Zaric or Blagoje Simic in their apartments, in their homes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I didn't know where Blagoje lived. First of all, I didn't know where Simo lived until I found out about that here. I knew that he lived somewhere in 62, that's what the name of that building was, but I didn't know any more details about that. I never went to either Simo's or Blagoje's home but that does not mean that Simo didn't visit me, he frequently came to the cafe and perhaps he even came to my flat. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to discuss the political life and that environment in the Samac municipality before the outbreak of the conflict. Could you please describe to us how did the appearance of a multi-party system in the territory of Yugoslavia make you feel and how was that reflected in the municipality of Samac and how did you relate those events with the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The events in the late 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you. Are you thinking of the late 1980s and the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking of the year 1989 and 1990 and I'm thinking about the 1998 or 1988 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please I'm concerned about this line of questioning. Of course I have no objection at all to Mr. Lukic leading evidence of the effect on Mr. Tadic himself and what he observed around him during the events involving the break-up of Yugoslavia. Of course he can speak directly to that and I have no problem with that, but I was wondering if Mr. Lukic intends to go into more general political matters concerning the break-up of Yugoslavia, in which case Mr. Tadic does not appear to be qualified to speak about those sorts of matters. Again, I repeat, if the object is to lead evidence concerning what Mr. Tadic himself experienced and saw, I've got no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Lukic understands the -- Mr. Di Fazio's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was very general and I have no intention of going into any kind of political polemic. It could be just a general question, how did he experience as a citizen the breakup of Yugoslavia and the situation and all these things that were happening around him.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: It's obvious that I was not a politically active person and that I'm not from that field and that I'm not an expert in that area, but in any case as an average citizen, I can have my own view and opinion and it's certainly not an expert or scientific opinion, but it's mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead and express it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So should I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, start.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In 1989, 1990, 1991, any objective observer could see that Yugoslavia will break-up. Of course, all of those who were in favour of Yugoslavia went through a very difficult time then and I counted myself amongst them because I spent all of my life in that Yugoslavia which was on its last legs. At that time, Yugoslavia broke apart into individual republics and it wasn't perhaps the actual break-up but it was a kind of break-up - and there was party activity within the republics unused to the multi-party system or more parties than one - all those who were heading those multi-party parties brought about quite bad relations amongst all of those participants. The programmes were mostly in the background. Everybody attacked everything and one of the most attacked things was that former Yugoslavia and communism which was supposed to leave the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what did you base your conclusions on? What was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The source of my information were television, radio, the newspapers, conversations with friends, acquaintances, even conversations that took part in -- that took place in the restaurant. There were those there who did have something significant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections in Bosnia and the victory of the national parties, what was your position on those policies and what was your knowledge about the programme of those parties and their activities? I'm thinking of the SDS, the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Already a lot has been said in the Chamber about that, about the victory of the national parties, not because they promised something better to the people who were hoping for something better, but because they were mostly trying to replace the to-date regime, that's what the abolishment of the communist system meant, that's what it was in the whole of Bosnia and that's what it was like in Samac. I wouldn't speak about the constituting of the organs of power, but I can say something about the people, individuals who came to certain posts. You heard that the president of the municipality was Mato Nujic, a person well known to me, he worked very close to my house at the medical centre. I never noticed that he excelled in anything in particular before those multi-party elections. The president of the executive board was Mirko Jovanovic, a completely unknown person in Samac. He -- even though he was born in Samac, in the Samac municipality, I found that out later. I think he came from Orasje or from somewhere and he became the president of the executive board. Vinko Dragicevic became the chief of the SUP. Other posts were also distributed in a similar fashion. Regarding Vinko Dragicevic since I knew all of his family very well from his grandfather down to him, his father, his uncles, I knew that family very well. He was quite qualified to be the chief of SUP, in a manner of speaking, because his grandfather was an Ustasa in the Second World War, World War II and it didn't bother me. I was on pretty good terms with his grandfather. However, Vinko did have one fault, his wife was a Serb and it was well-known that he wouldn't last long and that turned out to be true. He -- a man like him could not remain for long in such a responsible post. Ivo Kobas was mentioned here well, his wife was also a Serb and he was replaced and so on and so forth. As a citizen, I didn't have any special stance on this new division of power or this new authority. I worked just like I did before then, normally, I paid my taxes, I received various inspections, and this would probably have remained the same for a long time if the war hadn't broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, you said that you were on good terms with the Dragicevic family. Let us remind the Chamber what was the ethnicity of the Dragicevics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The Dragicevics were Croats. His father, Anto, who has also been mentioned in this courtroom, was one of those 14 who were in Belgrade, who were detained in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will discuss that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you mentioned concerning this gentleman Vinko Dragicevic, in fact, on page 22, lines 12 to 14, you said in your words: "He was quite qualified to be the chief of SUP, in a manner of speaking, because his grandfather was an Ustasa in the Second World War and it didn't bother me." I just wonder what you actually meant by that why he was qualified to be chief of the SUP in a manner of speaking because his grand dad had been a Ustasa in World War II and it didn't bother you. Maybe just very briefly you could just say a word or two or what you actually meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that he was qualified. I don't know how that can be translated. I said that he had a pedigree. I don't know how you can translate that into English, so he was predisposed, he had predisposition to get such a high post because the HDZ was a kind of continuation, the end product of a policy which was very painful for the Serbs in World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That seems to obviously be a translation problem that quite qualified and now Mr. Tadic has elaborated. Thank you, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also said that that was his grandfather and not his father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you also knew his grandfather, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his grandfather, grandfather Ivo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were you on good terms with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I visited him at his home often and I was also on good terms with all of his sons and his grandsons and Vinko was -- Vinko Dragicevic was one of those grandsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify this term "pedigree," in your opinion, the HDZ which was one of the participants in the organs of power, was it a recommendation if any of the forebearers were identified with the Ustasa movement in Croatia or came from it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In my humble opinion, yes, that's how it was because throughout that whole period, and the position of the HDZ to the various posts, this was evident. I didn't know Mato Nujic or his family so I cannot say anything particular about him, but about Vinko Dragicevic, I knew everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, have you heard of Yutel what is it, and did it play an interesting role in the political life in Samac during pre-wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: During the multi-party elections in Samac it wasn't only national parties that participated, there were other political parties as well such as Reformed Communists, Liberals and some other ones. Another party was the political party of Ante Markovic, I believe it was called Reformist Forces or something to that effect. At the time, Anto Markovic was prime minister of Yugoslavia. Prior to multi-party elections, he was prime minister of Yugoslavia. And he established this Reformist Forces party during that period of time and that party had quite a lot of supporters. It was quite active in Samac as well. A very good friend of mine was an advocate of that party and he tried to put up posters of Ante Markovic in my cafe. I objected to that and he said "Well, we're friends," and then I said to him that if he put up Ante Markovic's posters in my cafe, then everybody else would be entitled to doing the same and then my cafe would turn into a political campaign centre. Yutel stands for -- is an abbreviation and it stands for Yugoslav Television and Ante Markovic was especially frequently mentioned and popularised by that television station. However Ante Markovic's party did not achieve any significant results either in Samac or at the republic level or at the level of Yugoslavia itself. It achieved the least success in Croatia and was a bit more successful in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something else which is not directly linked to political life, but has something to do with that pre-war period of time. What was your attitude with respect to the orthodox church and is there anything you would like to tell us regarding the church?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Some time towards the end of 1991 or rather on the 13th of October, 1991, in the Serbian village called Donja Dubica a Serbian orthodox church was renewed, reconstructed and the patriarch came to bless the new place of worship and I was a kum or a patron during that ceremony and this is where I got to meet the patriarch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was patriarch at the time, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: It was Patriarch Pavle and he is patriarch to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what does this word "a kum to the church" mean and where is this village of Donja Dubica located, in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Donja Dubica is in Odzak municipality. At the time when the ceremony was held to consecrate the church, patriarch was the highest member of the clergy attending the ceremony and I as a kum or as a patron was the highest ranked civilian, layperson, attending the ceremony. A kumship has very deep roots among the orthodox people and a person who is a kum is held in respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the municipal authority function then in 1991 and what impact did it have on you as an ordinary member or citizen of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I've already said that there were no visible changes, simply the people in offices changed but the institutions remained the same, it's just that people at their helm were different. The rest of the staff working in institutions was the same. Inspectorate was probably one of the most interesting elements of administration for me because inspectors frequently come to inspect, to conduct controls and so on, and they started going in teams of two or three so that they would have Muslims and Croats in the team and so there wouldn't be any objections to the composition of the inspection team. For example, somebody could complain that the inspection team was composed of two Muslims or two Serbs and so on, so inspection teams took care to have a mixed composition. I knew some other people. I knew, for example, Izet Izetbegovic well, he was vice-president of executive council. I also knew Mirko Lukic who later after the negotiations became director of the inspectorate; however, I had no interests or no problems and therefore I seldom went to the municipal building at the time. I never had the honour of meeting officially Nujic or Mirko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the last name of --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: -- or Vinko Dragicevic. What I meant to say is that I never got to meet them officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please slow down, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the three names that you've mentioned. One of them was Nujic Mato, the second one was Mirko Jovanovic and the third one Vinko Dragicevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: These were the persons one would apply to if one had some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, you had -- you were businessman, you had a private catering establishment - we will return to that later - but this is what you did for a living; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I had a privately-owned catering establishment and that was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to something that we had described as incidents in the territory of Samac municipality. We've heard about that quite a lot but I would now like to ask you to describe what has impressed you the most, first of all concerning the war in neighbouring Croatia and the volunteers who took part in that war. What happened then, and what were the first information that reached you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Living at the border where on one side a war was waged and the other side lived in peace was not easy because everything would be reflected back and forth. So on both -- on two sides of the Sava River people simply held different views and the events had different repercussions on two different sides. For them, on the other side, it was perhaps normal to see somebody in a boat on the Sava River and they didn't think it was anything unusual to fire a few bullets at that person because, at the time, we still didn't have an established border going through the Sava River; however, for us, that event would have been quite shocking. During the war in Croatia, there were people who went to fight there as volunteers from our area and occasionally, they would come back either for leave or after they were permanently discharged, they would come in uniforms frequently and one could also frequently see them bearing arms so the situation perhaps didn't seem unusual for some people on the other side, but for us, who still held old-time views, the situation was very unusual. Those people who came from the front sometimes bearing arms, sometimes unarmed, usually provoked conflicts. I remember quite a number of such conflicts. I remember that in a coffee bar called kum, there was a scuffle between those guys and the owner Lazo Stanisic. I remember that in the discotheque called Cusa these guys would appear quite often and they would always make trouble and throw out the patrons that they didn't like. Once, they even started spreading a rumour that one of those guys had disappeared, disappeared, inverted commas, and they had accused soldiers of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army for that although there were none in the vicinity. I remember that on one occasion I sat in my friend's back yard, that was in 1991 in late fall, and a man came in uniform, armed, into the back yard of this relative of mine. I recognised the man, his name was Galic and he was from Odzak municipality. I knew him superficially, he greeted me, he said, "How are you going, Brko?" I responded because I thought it was wiser to respond as he was wearing a uniform and was armed. Then I asked him, "Why were you wearing uniform, why are you armed?" and he replied to me saying, "All of this area will be part of Croatia so there is no -- nothing unusual about me wearing uniform and weapons." So all of this created quite a tense environment for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What uniform did the man wear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: He wore the uniform of the National Guard Corps and those were Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the environment like on television, was there any propaganda, did you follow the news programmes and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The propaganda itself was worse than war. All of those things that did not take place in reality or during war were portrayed as having happened on television or in the press or were portrayed on television or in the press in much worse light; therefore, the television and the press had a major role in spreading fear and escalating tensions. I remember some other details and they were mentioned here as well so I will only touch upon them briefly. These soldiers had crossed over from Croatia to Samac municipality and disarmed some of our policemen. This has been described here. And under normal circumstances, this would be an unbelievable inconceivable event for some soldiers to come and disarm policemen, official policemen. And one of the witnesses here said that this was just a minor incident and that the weapons had been returned later on. I also remember that an acquaintance of mine who was drunk made a mistake and turned toward the bridge separating Bosanski and Slavonski Samac and as he approached the bridge, they opened fire upon him from heavy weapons and seriously injured him, although he was still on our side or rather on the part of the bridge belonging to Samac municipality. But despite of that, a policeman from Croatia took him by force to Slavonski Brod, to Croatia to take care of him there although Samac, Bosanski Samac and the health centre there was only a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which bridge do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The bridge over the Sava River between Slavonski Samac, which is in Croatia, and Bosanski Samac which is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned some wounding people having been wounded in a boat on the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Those were residents of Samac. I don't think I need to mention any names but they were simply riding in a boat along the river because we didn't have war on our territory, and as they rowed in a boat, people from Croatia started shooting at them. It was summertime and people went for a swim in the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone getting killed in a brick factory called Ciglana and what impact did that event have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: This event in Ciglana, the brick factory, had quite an impact upon the relations and the situation in town. Vujadin Goranovic [As interpreted] was a student of mine and he was in a town in the vicinity and a shell had been launched from Croatia and fell in the compound of the company where he was working. Several people were wounded and he got killed. Since his elder brothers were my students as well, I attended the funeral. His wife is a Croat and this complicated matters further. The situation was quite tense at that funeral. There were a lot of Croats and there were a lot of Serbs attending the funeral. I wouldn't like to go into the events in Sijekovac because that has been mentioned often and everybody by now knows what happened there and what impact that had on relations in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that event in Sjekovac was precisely at that period of time when this event with Goranovic took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when did the sabotage on the Sava River take place and what impact did that have on the life in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: There were sabotages from late 1991 and in early 1992. The bridge in Orasje was first destroyed which was the link between Tuzla and Zupanja. This was a very bad time and it's strange that somebody would think about knocking down such an imposing bridge over the Sava River. I think it was about 800 metres long. After that, the bridge over the Sava River in Samac was damaged. The bridge in Brcko was destroyed. I'm sorry that we are not able to show a document here sent by the Crisis Staff of Slavonski Brod from Croatia to Mr. Mato Nujic informing him that the bridge was mined and that if there is anything suspicious on the Samac side, they would blow up this bridge. This did happen later so that the bridge on the Sava River in Samac was blown up, it was mined and blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think there will be an opportunity to discuss this document later on in the proceedings. Could you please tell us the following, there are two events here that have been frequently described so I don't want to discuss them so much but just the consequences and how did you experience them. First of all, how did you experience the blowing up of Grga Zubak's kiosk?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Grga Zubak's kiosk and when it was blown up was something that upset all the citizens of Samac and everybody else because Grga Zubak's kiosk was in the parking of the SUP and there are always one, two or three duty officers in the SUP all the time who are constantly monitoring the parking so this was an additional upset to the population that it was possible to mine a kiosk, blow up a kiosk that was on the parking of the SUP and if that was possible then anything else is possible in other places. It was never found out who blew up the kiosk or the bridge or some other facilities even though the Samac bridge had 12 officers on duty who were guarding it around the clock and in spite of that the bridge was blown up, so it's not up to me to draw the conclusions. Another event that was mentioned here as well is the namesake of today's date and that is the Valentino Cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it happened on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened on the same day. I wouldn't want to talk about that too much, everything has already been said but I would like to mention a few things about a meeting that was held after that. There was a meeting held in the cinema hall because of that event and I attended this meeting. It's already been said who the speakers were at the meeting. I wouldn't want to talk about that, but at one point one citizen of Samac, Abdibegovic, stood up and proposed that the -- a memorial be built in the park for all the young men who were killed. Naturally, I thought that this was not an appropriate act. They are not people who would need a monument built for them in a park, but after that applause broke out and I understood that after that, you couldn't even think about opposing any idea of that kind and this actually indicates this collective identity of the people and so on that it is not possible to oppose such a collective opinion even though it's not right, but it's impossible to do anything in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we could go on a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume our proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We ended with the pre-war events in Samac, but I wanted to ask you a couple of more things unrelated to these incidents and this is something that His Honour Judge Lindholm asked you about when you mentioned the place where you surrendered. Could you please tell us what you know about those pre-war exchanges the exchange in the municipality of Samac, and did you have any direct contacts in this regard or do you have any direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Those events in 1991 have already been discussed here so I will just add some details. Samac, since the bridge in Orasje was already destroyed at that time, and in Brcko also, the only connection with Croatia was the bridge in Bosanski Samac and this is probably the reason why the two opposing sides, Yugoslavia and Croatia agreed to conduct the exchange of prisoners in Samac, prisoners and other persons at the time who happened to be on one or the other side. This was in late 1991 and there were several such exchanges. The witness Izet talked about this and he provided a lot of details about that because he was directly participating in it. I was curious about it, let me put it that way, so I went to see what these exchangers looked like and what was going on there. I saw the procedure, the International Red Cross and so on, and then after certain amount of time, a friend of mine came and she told me that her two sons were captured and that they were to be exchanged that day and she asked me, since she wasn't from that area, to go with her, because she didn't know where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. When you say after a certain period of time, this is still happening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is still 1991,, it was after the first exchange, so the second exchange happened after a certain amount of time and she asked me to go with her. So I went with her and then I was able to look at what was happening more immediately. Her two sons came, the International Red Cross was there, and when they came to say whether they wanted to be exchanged or not they said that they didn't want to go to the other side. The International Red Cross noted that down, and they came back to Samac with my friend and for a while, they spent some time in Novi Grad because that wife was from Novi Grad, that woman was from Novi Grad. So it was that principle of saying whether you wanted to be exchanged or not. The International Red Cross was distributing sandwiches there and so on so I could see a little bit about how these exchanges were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In early 1991, these incidents that you described, what were the consequences to the life in the city, what was the reaction to that? Was there a change in the way of life of all of those different ethnic groups in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: All of those things that happened in late 1991 and early 1992 had a lot of influence on the life in Samac. Some people were influenced more, some less, it depends how people took it. At the time, a lot of refugees had arrived from Croatia. They were either -- they either had family connections with Samac or they came there because they didn't have anywhere else to go. They were either taken in by their families and those who didn't have any relatives were accommodated in the houses of people who were willing to receive them. I also received a family into my household, a family that I didn't know from before. It was a husband and a wife and two young girls of high school age, approximately. And the school year, 1991/1992, they spent at my house. They went to the economics school in Samac. When war broke out in Samac, they went back to a part of Croatia where there were no combat operations. Many citizens, when the tensions were pretty high, tried to leave Samac to take their families out simply if it was possible, they tried to reduce as much as possible the number of their family there in case something should happen. I didn't have any feelings like that, I didn't have a sense of it. In the beginning I didn't think that there would be war and my personal feeling was that if anything should happen because based on the talk going round at the time, separation, line of division, and all of these international commissions and the cantonisation of Bosnia, I don't know, division into, let me call them cantons, I thought that this would take about 15 days, this division, and then everything would return to normal so I didn't try to do anything in terms of getting my family out or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you heard anything about the forming of the Serbian municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of being established, and if you did, what did you hear and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: This was precisely what I was talking about earlier. There were attempts to create new municipalities, new cantons, and something like that, so probably this formation of this Serbian municipality of Samac was another attempt along these lines. I did hear about it because the media did report that. It was no secret. They reported that the Serbian municipality of Samac was formed, that some bodies were formed, that the president of the assembly was elected and so on but I didn't pay any particular attention to that. I remember that an acquaintance of mine, a veterinarian, his wife worked with me at the school for a long time, he was the president of the municipality. Ilija Ristic, if you need for me to tell you his name, it was Ilija Ristic

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you hear about this man?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: That he was the president of the assembly of the Serbian municipality of Samac but he continued to work at the veterinarian centre, the station, he continued to carry out the duties that he had been carrying out until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any other officials of this new municipality, did you hear about the police, were there any stories about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I heard that Stevan Todorovic was appointed chief of that police, the chief of police. I didn't attach an importance to that either because he had already been the chief of this other police that was in Samac so that was the police that was operating regularly. There was no other police other than the police that was operating in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. I heard you say when you mentioned the name Stevan Todorovic, a chief without the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was a chief but he didn't have any police, he didn't have a station, he didn't have the regular organs that the police usually have -- has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was being talked about in town about him being appointed chief of police, were there any comments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were comments because nobody was very happy about this choice. Other people knew him much better than I did, some neighbours at whose house he used to live as a student, a high school student, they especially commented this as being a very unfortunate choice and they said things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any change sensed in the life in Samac after the constituting of this new municipality, the declaration of this Serbian municipality of Samac? Did you sense anything?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I said in the interview and I can repeat that again, that this didn't have any effect on me, not me, but life in general in Samac. We all continued to be citizens of that municipality, the municipality of Samac. We all carried out our work and other duties in the municipality of Samac. I went to the municipality to get certain decisions, I paid my taxes, nothing substantially changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During those first few months of 1992, where did your information come from about the work of political parties? Earlier you mentioned that you got information from television, but did you go to party meetings, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not attend any meetings, any party meetings, maybe I went to one or possibly two. There was that movement for Yugoslavia, so in those terms, I went to see what they were advocating. There was a rally in front of the hotel and I think that those parties, I don't know whether it was one party, but there were several parties which were in favour of Yugoslavia, whether it was the Reformist Parties or the Reformed Communist party, I don't remember, but I remember that quite a few speakers at the time said things: Mesud Nogic, Marko Filipovic, that they said a woman spoke on behalf of the trade unions, she was in the trade union organisation at the time, and some other citizens also spoke. If I'm not mistaken I think that Ibela Salkic also said something, Ibrahim Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in favour of preserving Yugoslavia at the time? What were your views concerning the developments at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I had spent my entire life in Yugoslavia and it wasn't easy for me to see it disintegrate. They -- there was mention of a rump Yugoslavia at the time and I was in favour of even of that rump Yugoslavia, that was better than nothing. There were even some arrangements or agreements made to that effect and they came quite close to creating the rump Yugoslavia; however, the SDS -- the SDA abandoned the idea at the very end and then other things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you learn that the SDA abandoned the idea, gave up on the idea?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I learned that through the media. I wasn't involved in any of this; however, I learned through the media that a party, I believe it was called MBO, it was established by a Muslim intellectual Zulfi Karpasic who lived in Switzerland, he set up that political party which had quite a lot of influence among the Muslim nation, he advocated and was trying to talk Alija Izetbegovic into accepting that concept. I believe that Alija even agreed to this and attended -- no, I think it was Zulfi Karpasic who attended negotiations concerning this; however, in the end all of that fell through. I learned of this also through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all I needed to know, how did you learn about this? Now I would like to turn to another topic. The following topic I would like to discuss is the 4th detachment. I don't think that there is any question about you having been a member of the 4th detachment. Now please tell us, how and when did you become a member of the 4th Detachment and what do you know about its creation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The situation was quite tense at the time and the forces attempting to preserve Yugoslavia used all kinds of approaches. One of the approaches was the Yugoslav Peoples' Army which could have been the force that could have implemented it and several things were done to further that including the mobilisation of conscripts into the reserve forces of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. This is how the mobilisation came about, the mobilisation of all citizens. Those who responded, those who believed that that was the right solution and responded to the call-up and were consequently mobilised. Some citizens did not respond to the call-up for whatever reasons. A number of Muslims were among them and the majority of Croats did not respond to the call-up either. It hasn't been mentioned here that a large number of Serbs failed to respond to mobilisation too. According to something I learned of later, about 700 conscripts at the time deserted, this is how we referred to it in popular terms, they left and went either to Serbia or they went abroad, simply changed their place of residence, so a number did not respond to the call-up but the majority did and this is how I came to join the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was about to object because it wasn't clear at all to me from that answer that the witness, whether the witness was talking generally or about specifically about what happened in Bosanski Samac. I understand though from that last part of his answer that he is confining his comments to events that he saw and observed and experienced in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My comments mostly pertain to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the number, the figure that you mentioned, 700, that strictly pertains to Bosanski Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean the town of Samac itself, I meant the municipality of Samac. I don't know how to define that geographic term. It's an entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was, when did you receive your call-up papers and what happened following that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: As I have told you, that was in early 1992. Head of the Secretariat for National Defence was my former student, Milos Bogdanovic, a very nice man, and I believe that he and I were on very good terms. We would always greet each other, exchange a few words and so on. On one occasion, he called me and told me that I would be mobilised and he suggested that due to certain circumstances, I should accept a post involving logistics in the 4th Detachment and I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was your position in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: It's already been said that I was assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I never received any kind of appointment document appointing me assistant commander but logically concluding I was appointed by commander of the 17th Tactical Group which was a unit superior to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Commander was Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he an active officer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: He was an officer of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, an active one. It's already been mentioned but let me reiterate again that he, with other officers, on the 19th of May left our area because he originally hailed from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've heard the names of other senior people in the 4th Detachment already, we don't have to go into that, but I'm interested in something else. Before the war, before joining the 4th Detachment, did you socialise with Radovan Antic who we know to be the commander of the 4th detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I knew Radovan Antic quite well, however, we didn't socialise. We weren't family friends or anything of the like but we knew each other quite well. Before the war, he was head of the SUP for a while and that drew us apart to a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now tell us about Jovo Savic who we know to have been deputy commander, did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I am acquainted with Jovo Savic as well, he lived in my neighbourhood, we didn't socialise but we knew each other as neighbours. He would frequently come to my cafe, unlike Radovan Antic who never stepped into my cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already described your relationship with Zaric. Now tell us, what did you learn and from whom about your tasks in the 4th Detachment. You've discussed this in your interview but we'd like you to go into that again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Radovan Antic, therefore, he informed me of all of my tasks. There was no chain of command whereby command of the 17th Tactical Group would issue orders to me. No, it wasn't like that. I was immediately informed of this by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you do in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: There were no particular tasks and duties at the time. If there was any meeting of the command, I would attend the meeting and see whether there were any orders. Sometimes they would inform us of a problem or similar things along those lines. I remember that once or twice, we went to the range to shoot, meaning that the members of the 4th Detachment went to the range to fire and my task was to secure a bus that was to take the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend that fire practice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did on one occasion, but I believe I didn't go the second time. It was held in the vicinity of Brcko where there was a military facility, a military range that was a secure facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you issued with a weapon in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: All of those who were members of the 4th Detachment were issued a weapon by that formation as well as uniforms, based on availability. That means, all of us who were members of that formation received weapons but not all people received uniforms. The uniforms were the old Yugoslav-type uniforms, SMB, olive-green uniforms. They were the same as the uniforms of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. And when I say formation weapons, I mean that certain weapons were intended for certain units so I was assistant commander for logistics. In my unit, I was entitled to a pistol, and therefore, I was issued with a pistol that was typically issued to people in such posts in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. I think it was TP type 69 or something similar to that. The soldiers were issued rifles, machine-guns or I don't know how it was decided who should receive what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who conducted the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The distribution of weapons was carried out by the logistics service of the 17th Tactical Group. That was an organised unit of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army which had all of the resource a unit of that nature should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were the headquarters of that logistics service?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they give the weapons to you or to company commanders within the detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: It depends. They would give it sometimes to me, I would sign a receipt and since I never had any weapons before that, I was given a receipt saying that this pistol had been issued to me and the pistol was the property of the 17th Tactical Group and should somebody ask for, I was supposed to show that receipt. And other people received formation weapons and also signed a receipt for them so that they had a justification, a legal basis for possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who gave weapons to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: They would be issued with weapons either in Pelagicevo or they would be given weapons directly by their immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you issued with a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I was issued with a uniform and a jacket, a winter-type jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how frequent were the meetings that you attended? Let me ask you first ask you something that was frequently mentioned here: Where were the headquarters of the 4th Detachment command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this, I have to tell you that the 4th Detachment operated publicly, transparently. It was no secret organisation which met in dark corners and negotiated things or acted in that manner. It was a publicly-promoted unit of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and it had its HQ in a place that was called Work Organisation Sit, Work Unit Mladost.
