This Work Unit Mladost had an administrative building and in there, there was several offices that were used by the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on we'll take a look at the picture and comment upon this further, but now please answer my previous question. How frequently did you attend meetings in the command of the 4th Detachment starting in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The meetings were not frequent because there was no need to hold them. They would usually be held as needed. For example, we had to have a meeting before going to the shooting range and we had a meeting regarding that. And then after the shooting range, we held a meeting to analyse what had happened there. I remember also that there was several public gatherings or rallies in the town of Samac. I'm now referring strictly to the town of Samac because the 4th detachment operated only in the town of Samac. I remember that several of those public gatherings were held at which members of the 4th detachment spoke informing both the members of the 4th detachment and those who were non-members as well as those who attended the gatherings because those gatherings were public. I remember that one was held in the memorial hall. I believe that I didn't attend that one whereas another gathering was held at the Tekstilac factory. I was there as an observer listening to the people who spoke there. So that was no secret. And to go back to your question, the meeting were -- the meetings were held when there was a need for them. And they probably weren't more frequent than once or twice a month, but since the headquarters of the 4th Detachment were immediately next to my house, actually across the street from my house, I went there often. I would just go there, sit down, have some coffee with the people, chat, or invite them over to my place for coffee. This was nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you about your relationship with the leaders of the 4th Detachment. Did you meet Stevan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you can bring your chair a little bit closer. If you need a break, Mr. Tadic, just tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't need a break, but the chair is very uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you met him. How frequently did you see him in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I met him at one of the meetings of the 4th Detachment when he would come and I would see him from time to time when meetings were scheduled. He didn't often come to meetings of the 4th Detachment because he was a commander maybe. I don't know how many detachments there were, there were at least 15, so if he constantly toured all of those detachments, then he would have to go to one or the other detachment practically every other day so there was no need for me to see him every other day. When he came, then I would see him when he would come to this meeting or for other talks and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just in order to follow the evidence clearly, is the witness saying there were 15 detachments within the 17th Tactical Group? That's what I understood him to be saying and I'd just like to be clear about that and I think the Chamber should be clear about that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said perhaps 15 because here in this court, we talked about the detachment that were in the Samac municipality, but the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group was much broader. There was Pelagicevo, Brkco, Orasje and I don't know what other locations were within the zone of the 17th Tactical Group so it wasn't just Samac, it was much broader. But I don't know how many detachments there were in each municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I assume that you know how many detachments there were in the Samac area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In the area of Samac, there were four or five detachments. Some documents or some places mention four and some mention five detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know those who headed the other detachments in the Samac territory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I knew them but not especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Nikolic come to your cafe to the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't because at that time, and I have to say that here, the active personnel of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army was something -- or the arrival of the active personnel of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army was an irritant to the population so because of my cafe and because of myself, he avoided doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your son, also called Miroslav, was he a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, my son, even though he's a reserve officer, was just a regular soldier in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was also often mentioned here, but I have to ask you about that also, what was the ethnic composition of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I said that mobilisation documents were sent to everybody and those who responded were members of the 4th Detachment and a lot of Serbs responded, a lot of Muslims and a lot of Croats. The fewest of those were the Croats because there was the fewest Croats in the actual town of Samac themselves. There were more Muslims and then there were even more Serbs. I don't know exactly what the percentages were but I believe that they were discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those meetings and those public rallies during which the 4th Detachment was mentioned, according to your knowledge, what was the purpose of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the 4th Detachment, as part of the JNA, was the protection of the constitutional order at the time of that state, and if you applied that to the 4th Detachment, then that would mean protection from infiltration by some unknown forces into our territory because we were immediately next to a state where there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about an attack on the town or was there talk about an imminent attack on the town? Was such an attack to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The town could have been attacked only from the Republic of Croatia across the bridge, the only bridge over the Sava River that was still standing, or possibly an attack could come from our western side across the River Bosna which was less probable but still possible because a large number of villages on that side border on Croatia and their ethnic composition was such, and it wasn't very difficult to cross the Sava with the appropriate technical means. In Samac, we could hear from our houses the movements of units, we could hear tanks or a vehicle or a group of vehicles when such vehicles were moving, you could hear that across the water. We could hear it very well and probably the people on the other side could hear if something was going on on our side, and usually if there was a movement of tanks, if there were five or six tanks moving, you could hear that. My house -- and we will see that later when I talk about that -- was positioned in such a way that from the balcony of my house, I could see a large part of Slavonija and that would be in the area of the so-called Sljuncara that was a part where they extracted gravel from the river so there was some cranes and other equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the village of Prud which you mentioned -- well, you didn't mention it but that village is on the other side of the River Bosna on the other end of the bridge, we know that from before. Were there any special forces there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I had a lot of acquaintances in Prud even friends. My brother is married to a woman from Prud so I was in Prud quite frequently and I had a large number of acquaintances there, and on one occasion a friend of mine from Prud told me -- this friend actually cut timber, and he told me that about 30 young men had arrived in Prud who were to cut timber, but later it turned out that they were actually instructors who had come there to Prud to possibly train members of those units, units that were to be formed in Prud. So those members later at checkpoints -- because later it turned out that they stood watch at checkpoints along with the members of the population. I would frequently pass by that way and always somebody from Prud, one of the citizens from Prud was always there so I didn't have any problems. Sometimes they would check the trunk of my car to see if I didn't have any weapons or anything like that but they would usually allow me to pass through in contrast to others who did have some unpleasant encounters with those people. The situation was similar in the area of Samac. In the same way before the hostilities would break out in all villages, regardless of whether they were Croat or Serb, some kind of control was set up and everybody felt it was their right to monitor the others or those who were passing through. This was not a nice practice. There were not too many incidents on the -- on those roads. I never had anything happen to me, but others did. But it was a very uncomfortable situation because it was still peacetime. It was uncomfortable to have incidents like this happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to go back to the 4th Detachment again, to the command, your command. The meetings that you attended, were you tasked with what you would do specifically should an attack take place, did you receive any instructions about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I specifically didn't have any particular task. If it did exist, it was probably something that the commander had and it was under seal. I'm not a military expert, but I think that the usual procedure is that the orders are kept by the commander and if the situation calls for it, he opens those instructions up and sees what the tasks are or he receives the tasks from the commander at a given time. I personally didn't have any nor did I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection to the latter part of the answer, but the witness there seems to me is purely speculating. Mr. Lukic's question was, with respect, quite clear. He asked: Did you -- were you tasked about what you should specifically do should an attack take place? Now, the witness can say yes or no but can't speculate as to whether commanders had sealed off or had sealed instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, the witness should discuss what actually happened, and what he did, and what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I think that I clearly said that I personally didn't have any task. I don't know whether that was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was recorded, but then you said "probably the commander," but we won't discuss the -- did you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't personally and I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, I take it from that answer that therefore the witness is saying, and Mr. Lukic may care could clarify this, that the 4th Detachment had no specific instructions as to what to do, publicly known, that is known amongst the members of the 4th Detachment of instructions of what to do in the event of an attack, no one knew what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is perhaps a topic for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you have any instructions and now I'm asking you, which is also something that interests the Prosecutor, did other members of the 4th Detachment know what to do if there should be an attack? Did you know anything personally about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I just answered this question in my answer that the tasks are not given in advance in the army to anybody to say, well, you have such and such an assignment if such and such a thing should happen. Such instructions are not given in the army. If something happened, the commander had that and he didn't carry that in his pocket. It was placed, stored, somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is another topic that was -- that related to that period. Did you hear anything about the arrival of the men to the village of Batkusa and what is your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Also from stories that circulated, which is inevitable in situations like that, especially when two helicopters land in a small village, everybody knows about it and everybody talks about it, so based on those stories I knew that I think two helicopters landed in the village of Batkusa and some people arrived in those helicopters. At the time, I didn't know anything more detailed about that. Now at this time I know much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Chamber is interested about what you know at the time so we will stick to that, not to what you found out later. Did you know at the time where those people came from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I knew then that these people came from Yugoslavia because everybody said that those helicopters were helicopters of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment in your command, did -- was anything said about those people in connection with their arrival?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was talk that they arrived. We were informed that they arrived. We were told about it at a meeting in the office. I don't think that it was an official meeting, but we were just told that they had arrived and I think that the commander said that they will not be coming to Samac and that they will not have any contact with the 4th Detachment. I think that that was what was said, that they will not have any contact with the 4th Detachment because the 4th detachment is of the composition that we had already talked about and this is something that didn't suit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Tadic, when you say that the people who came on the two helicopters came from Yugoslavia, which part of Yugoslavia, could you be specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean geographically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Well not from Serbia, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the different republics of the former Yugoslavia, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said from Yugoslavia, I believed it to be the Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I understood that, but just for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to ask the witness, about when was that when they arrived, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could tell you now that it was on the 11th of April, 1992, but this is something that I learned about later but at the time, the general notion that it was in early April, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we know the names of many of the people whom we will mention later, but some of those specials from Serbia, have you ever met them after the break out of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: You mean after?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after. Just tell me yes or no because we will come back to that later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Before the 17th of April, I did not have occasion to come across them and after the 17th of April, I had a number of unpleasant encounters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have you already gave me an answer to what I was going to ask you. When you saw them after the 17th of April, did you remember ever seeing some of them in your Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, I can assure you that none of them had ever stepped into Cafe AS before the 17th and I had never seen any of them in Samac before the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to your Cafe AS which has been mentioned a great deal in this trial. Although this can be found in your interview, let us repeat this here before the Trial Chamber. When did you open your Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps later on, I will have an opportunity to elaborate on how I stopped being a teacher and became a caterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe this is the right time to say -- to explain that in a few words only.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: One of the witnesses here before this Trial Chamber already mentioned this and said that the Cafe AS had been confiscated from me, the premises in which Cafe AS are located. That was sometime in the 1970s. At the time, those who enriched themselves were subject to persecution and a law from 1949 was invoked. According to that law, an individual could not own premises larger than 76 square metres. In the meantime, I had obtained a permit from the municipality. I attached the draft, the building construction draft and so on, and I built this facility which had 83 square metres. The authorities in Samac measured the facility and said that I could not own the premises as such, and they confiscated it from me without paying any compensation to me. The decision was adopted in 1974 or 1975, the decision concerning this. At that time, approximately, I met the uncle of Izet Izetbegovic and since he was a judge and we had some kind of administrative court and he was a judge of the administrative court and therefore, I petitioned the administrative court regarding this; however, it was to no avail. We even wrote to Tito at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we move to the events that matter, we don't want the details which are quite unrelated to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This issue might be important for an incident that took place later on but we don't have to go into this. Please tell us, briefly, so you opened a shop following that, and tell us, when was this shop closed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: After all of these difficulties, the premises were returned to me under the condition that I was not allowed to sell it or lease it but rather only to run the premises myself and this is how I stopped working in the school and opened a shop. I opened a shop in 1983, both my wife and I stopped working and started operating this shop which we ran up until 1986 or 1987 and after that I closed the shop and opened the cafe and this cafe operates now a days as well. I simply wanted to give an explanation how it all came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you needn't have gone into all those details. So the cafe was opened in 1987. Let us take a look at the photograph first and then you can explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown photograph D2/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could you please describe this photograph to us? What important things can we see in this street this is Edvard Kardelj Street?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes it was called Edvard Kardelj Street before now it's called Cara Dusana Street and this direction here leads to Modrica whereas the town itself is on the opposite side. This facility here is my house. From this angle, one cannot see the cafe because this here is grapevine covering the front garden and behind this yellow fence is where the garden is, the cafe garden, the open area where we keep tables in summertime. Right next to this bicycle is a small gate, this part here. I hope we shall see another photograph later on. So this small gate shows the entrance into my house and this was explained yesterday. So through this small gate, one enters the house in which I live and then this larger gate further on is where you enter the cafe premises. So these are two completely separate premises that have nothing in common except for the foundations. And this building here across the street is the work unit Mladost, a part of the Sit Factory, this is where the kitchen is belonging to the Mladost work unit and these upper two windows is where the premises of the 4th Detachment were. These two windows here. Between these two buildings is a passage, some 8 metres wide, and behind that, there are flag posts there. On holidays, state-owned companies had to raise flags, and this is where flag posts were where flags were flying. One couldn't see these flag posts because they were inside in the passage, but if one paid attention, one could see the flags flying on flag posts. The kiosk there, I'm showing it right now, is the kiosk owned by two guys who will later on come to be mentioned as detainees in this case. So this is a kiosk, a green grocer kiosk that they ran.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be wise to have the witness indicate all of these places with a number rather than describing all of that for the record. Perhaps it would be easier if he put a number next to each house or would you rather have me describe it for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps the numbers would be much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number one next to the place where the entrance into your house is -- oh, no, put rather number 1 next to your house.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the entrance leading into your house, put number 2 there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And entrance into the garden of your cafe, put a number 3 there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better if you drew arrows on the sidewalk so that this can be clear.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, it's quite clear on the photograph as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Then put number 4 on the windows of the 4th Detachment command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put 5 where the flag posts were.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we need to now describe it for the record and enumerate all of these places or is this clear as it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's clear because he is following your description.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The only other thing, I think, Your Honour, was the kiosk. I don't think that's been pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The witness spoke about the kiosk and you can see it in the photograph and there's no number on the photograph so I thought for the sake of completeness we should put a number there to make all of his evidence understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another photograph here which that was given to me by the accused today. I believe it is a much better photograph and it would be good to show the photograph as well. We could scan it tomorrow and have it admitted into evidence because it depicts quite well the issue that we discussed yesterday, the entrance into the cafe AS. I have told the Prosecutor before we started the hearing today that this photograph could be quite useful to us and I know that it can be enlarged by the technical booth so I don't know, should we show it now or leave it for tomorrow or rather for Monday and enlarge it by then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think when you've completed the business you want to do with it, like enlarging it, also giving copies to the Prosecution so we can have it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could you please describe Cafe AS to us? What did the premises look like, and if necessary, we could also draw a sketch, but for the time being, could you describe it for us first?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Cafe AS has a bit more than 80 square metres and it consists of three parts, so to speak. Could I please be given a piece of paper so that I can sketch it? It would be clearer if I drew a sketch. The front room --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: So this is where one would enter the front office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put a number 1 next to it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: All right, I did. Then number 2 would be the bar. And right here, there's an opening, it's not a door just an opening through which one gets into the next room which is a bit smaller. And then right here in this area, there's a staircase leading to the basement which is about this size. So number 5 would be the basement. It's about four by four metres. And then number 6 is the bathroom. This front area is where there was a television and then the tables and chairs are along the wall and then in the middle is the pool table. So the people who sit in the front room, they sit at these chairs that are lined up against the wall and then people shooting pool would be around the table and those who watch TV would be in this area here. Now, in this other part, there are four tables, four tables which were used by people who wanted to have a more intimate atmosphere, have a drink, play cards or something like that. And here, in the basement area, in the lower area, there were two more tables. That's more or less what it was like. This part here was taken from this area here because the stairs there lead upstairs to my apartment so those two parts are not connected. The entrance here is the entrance to my apartment so when I would be going into my apartment, I would go inside here, I would climb up the stairs and go to my apartment. This -- these premises here have nothing to do with the upstairs part. If you wanted to go to the upstairs part, you have to come out here and go upstairs here through this entrance. If I wanted to go to the cafe from my apartment, I would come out this way, come outside, come around here, and enter the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a door between this large room and the room marked with the number 4?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: This number 3 indicates just a passage. There is no door between those two rooms so it's just a passage way. You cannot close it or lock it because there is no door. Also, there is no door either to go downstairs. Anyone who comes in here can go also downstairs because there is no door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any other way to enter that downstairs room other than from that room marked with number 4?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No. There was no way to enter this room other than through the entrance marked by an arrow. There are two small windows here, very small windows, maybe 50 by 70 size, and they were from reinforced glass so you cannot see through the glass if you're inside looking outside, nor can you see from the outside inside the room through the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the shelter there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. When I talk about the civilian protection, I will probably talk about the shelter. Here, in front of my house, there is a fence. We saw that on the photograph and here is the entrance to my house and here is the entrance to the cafe. There was a tree here and there was an arrow on that tree, a large arrow that had the word shelter written on it and later I will talk about all this. Anyway, it said shelter on that arrow and anybody who was nearby when the shelling started -- there is a bus station here in front of my house here by this door going in one direction and then across the street near the kiosk is the other bus stop which goes -- which is for buses going from Samac to the villages. So it's only the transportation to the villages around Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will talk about that later but this arrow, can you please mark it with the number 7. Could you indicate the entrance to your house with the number 8?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: So all of those people who happened to be around here, whether they are at the bus stop or thereabouts, would run into the cafe. If the shelling was more intense, then they would run into this room marked with the number 4 because it was more sheltered, there were no windows along this wall so it was more protected here. But for those who were very afraid, they, then, could go downstairs to the room marked 5 and then they could spend the time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we can tender this floor plan into evidence. Is it necessary to describe what it all means? Perhaps it would be clearer if I explained what is marked by what number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just have marked the pool table. Can we have that marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark that please with the number 9?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Number 1. Yes, can I say it, because I can find it much easier to get around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as long as you do it a little faster?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is the entrance to the Cafe AS; number 2 is the bar; number 3 is the passage from the first room into the second room; number 4 is the second room; number 5, the cellar; number 6, toilet; number 7, sign indicating the shelter; number 8, entrance to the apartment; and number 9 is the pool table.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document now -- this exhibit now be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D144/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And what title do we give it, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a sketch of the AS Cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Tadic, we will talk about the AS Cafe, but all the questions will be relating to the relevant period, that is the year 1991 and the first few months of 1992. What were the work hours of the cafe, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The cafe was open from -- well, it was actually open nonstop, as they say, and that's how it was mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude, I do not want to suggest anything, but can we say that for as long as anybody was sitting inside, anybody else could come in and enter the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard a lot of testimony here that a lot of cards were played in the cafe before the war. Was there any card playing and what kind of cards were played?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war and even now, after the war, card games are played in the cafe and this is not the only cafe in Samac where you can play cards. Perhaps the name is wrong, a cafe, actually, my place is not a cafe really but it's called that because it's the easiest name to give it, but it's actually not a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how would you define it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In my permit, work permit, it's called a snack bar, that's how it's been described ever since it was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any gambling there or was it just card games the way witnesses described it as part of a social interaction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, there were other entertainments too. In our law, it states that gambling is not prohibited unless it's a business. If it's a business, then it's illegal, it's prohibited so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it usual in Samac for people to play cards in restaurants and cafes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In several cafes, yes. There was a socially-owned place we called it a Dascara, and it was part of a hotel, and that's where card games were also played all day and late into the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you whether the officers from the 4th Detachment dropped by and you answered my question. Did members of the 4th Detachment stop by at your cafe and did anybody come bearing arms, were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: We've already said that members of the 4th Detachment were armed but they were not allowed to carry the weapons around town. They were used only in case there was a mobilisation or if they were going somewhere on assignment. So the weapons were not meant to be carried around, nor was the uniform of dress uniform, something that you could parade around in. They were requisites which you could use only certain circumstances so nobody came to the AS in uniform or with weapons. As far as visits to my place, everybody came. I didn't even have to know out of 500 people who were the members of the 4th Detachment. Those whom I knew very well, I knew that they were in the 4th Detachment, I knew those people -- some people I knew very well and I knew that they were not in the 4th Detachment, but these things never bothered anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the period immediately prior to the outbreak of the conflict on the 16th of April. During those days in March and April, did all ethnic groups come to your cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Until the 16th of April, the day of the 16th of April, everybody would come to my cafe. There was one of the Dragicevics who played cards in my cafe, even the person mentioned here Truman, the two of them actually played cards and this is something that this Dragicevic told me about later. During the war, AS was one of the safest places and anybody who wanted to could come here and this is the situation to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any prominent people come to your cafe as well, people prominent in the political life, people who were of Croat or Muslim ethnicity, did they also come to your cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The prominent politicians at that time were not prominent before that period so at the time, they were in the multi-party elections so it turned out that they were prominent people, but all the people who were mentioned mostly did frequent the cafe. Some came more often and some did not and some never came at all such as, for example, Sulejman Tihic, Dragan Lukac already mentioned here, but many of the witnesses who were here were even regular patrons and they came very often. There is no need to mention them because they, themselves, have stated here that they used to come to the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the episode told by Salkic about your son preventing an incident involving him; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I remember Ibrahim talking about it. I was very -- I was on very good terms with that family, the Salkic family to this very day, but I wasn't there at the time when this happened. My son told me about it later and I have no doubt that it happened the way he said but the practice was that if I wasn't there, my son was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it time for a break now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will continue at 1805 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Can we stop the witness 15 minutes before time so that we deal with other matters which I've been informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, do you remember among the guests in your cafe, were there any policemen and what was the ethnicity of those policemen, if they came?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The cafe, I call it that, just like everybody else does, everybody came to the Cafe AS, policemen were frequent guests at any time of the day or night. Frequently they were in uniform and very often they were also in civilian clothes. One of them who I remember with pleasure was killed, unfortunately. His name was Lugar Gregurevic and he would come to the cafe practically every day, Mijo Ljoljic, Savo Cancarevic, Simo Krunic and many others, many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A small assistance. I see here in the transcript on page 67, line 25, it says Lugar Gregurevic and because we know that this nickname is connected to another person. Maybe it would be good to make this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Clarify who this person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person who killed him is mentioned, what is the name of the policeman who came to the cafe often?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The name of the police officer is Luka Gregurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: In early May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about his killing, who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: He was killed in the -- in a place called Crkvina, something that is talked about a lot here in the warehouse where the infamous crime was committed by Lugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you were good friends?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are some other names here. You mentioned Savo Cancarevic, police officer, Simo Krunic, and Mijo Ljoljic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Mijo Ljoljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is he also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to move into a private session, but the witness Fitozevic mentioned in private session four names so if it's necessary, maybe we could go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any Yugoslav insignia in the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the other part of the premises that I've already shown, I believe it's marked with number 4, there was a large photograph of Tito there, 80 by 50 centimetres and it stayed there all the way up until mid-May. It hung there until May and on one occasion, I had to remove it promptly and I will probably be given an opportunity to explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later. I would like to stay with the Cafe AS although turn to a different period of time. Can you tell us whether Cafe AS operated during the war, starting on April 16th and throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Cafe AS did work during the war when it was possible, when it was permitted. It was quite active from the second half of 1992. I think that other cafes were open during that time and it was operating quite actively after that so from mid-1992 and on, until the end of the war. It is obvious that permits were needed in order to reopen cafes and although we had a continuity, we still had to obtain a permit from the municipality to reopen the cafe. I was given such permit to continue the operation of the cafe. However, I have to point out something peculiar about Cafe AS. At the time when the war started, there was no communication with Odzak municipality. My entire family lived there, as did relatives of many of my friends, acquaintances and relatives who were not in the area so that all of them would gather in Samac, not all at the same time, obviously, but occasionally, every couple of days or so, they would come and gather in large numbers since they had no accommodations, since they didn't know anybody in Samac who would be closer to them than me, then they would gather in my cafe. They had no accommodation in Samac and therefore, we put up sponge mattresses in the lower part of the cafes -- of my cafe and in the other part of the cafe and some 20 of them or more would sleep there. We also provided blankets for them. Some of them slept upstairs in the rooms that were not used by me, the rooms that were used by my son and some of them slept in the cafe. So the cafe was not operating, so to speak, however, it wasn't shut down either, people were simply housed there, if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you didn't run it as a catering establishment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, no. While there was still some juices there left and other drinks, they used it up and since supplies were not refurbished, there was nothing there else to consume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need to put an exhibit before you, but can you tell us whether there was a ban on liquor sale or do you think there is a need for the exhibit to be put on ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: No, there is no need for that. There was a ban on liquor sale; however, it wasn't efficient. It didn't bring about the desired outcome. Bootlegging was rampant just like in any war. One could obtain a certain kind of brandy called Ludara [phoen]. It was brought in from Serbia and it wasn't of good quality, it wasn't expensive but it was very unhealthy. So it wasn't impossible to get drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what does this term Ludara mean, why was this brandy called that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Because even small quantities of it would drive a man crazy let alone large quantities of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where was this brandy sold, and alcohol in general?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: It was sold in secrecy in the marketplaces and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more question and we will complete the Cafe AS topic. In addition to providing accommodation to people from Odzak, did you also put up some other people in your house and, if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: A large number of people, mostly from Odzak municipality went through my house and my cafe. Some women with young children who had come through an exchange, I believe it was on the 4th or 5th of July, stayed there for some ten days before finding another accommodation. There was a woman there who was a relative of my wife's and her friend who had been exchanged while their husbands remained in prison there. There was some other people as well. My uncle was there for a while and some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, as early as April, perhaps on the 18th or 19th of April, a car stopped in front of my house and I just happened to be downstairs and I saw a fellow citizen of mine, his name was Rizo Dzakic and he worked in the city waste disposal company and his wife was with him and I asked them, "What are you doing?" And they told me,"Well, can't you see what the situation is like? We're fleeing into Modrica." And then I asked them, "Well who can guarantee to you that the same won't happen in Modrica tomorrow?" And they said, "We don't know." And I asked them "Well, why are you going then?" And they said, "Well, we are afraid," and I told them, "Well, if you are afraid, why don't you come in and stay with me." I knew Izeta well. They were about ten years older than me and they were not really in any shape to travel so I told them, "Why don't you stay with me until the situation calms down," and they agreed. So they came upstairs to my apartment and Rizo and my wife spent the entire 15, 20 days or a month sitting in the corridor and smoking. That was the safest place as there was no windows there. They cooked some food for themselves there and spent 15 to 20 days there. Then they went back to their own apartment and remained in Samac throughout the war. Their son also remained in Samac. He had a work obligation he had to discharge. Their daughter-in-law remained there as well throughout the war and is still there to this day. She has a shop in Samac. Rizo died some time in 1996 during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have to go into that. Mr. Tadic, please tell us, what happened, what did you hear, what did you see during the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992? Start with the evening, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, as I have mentioned, my cafe was open, my cafe, as I said, was open as usual. There was no tension, nothing unusual. It was mostly middle-aged people who came. Young people sometimes came and shot pool, but mostly it was the middle-aged people and elderly who came. And on that evening there were many people there, my acquaintances, friends, Serbs, Croats, the Muslims, they played cards, shot pool, some people left earlier and some of them remained until late that night. We were there until that time at about 2.30 when we heard the shooting. Since we were locals, we could tell that the shooting was coming from the direction of the bridge. People got up promptly and went home. Those who had cars went in their cars. Those who lived nearby walked and some people who lived quite a way remained there. I remember two guys, one of them had a house about a kilometre and a half from Samac and the other one lived at about the same distance and they were sons of a friend of mine. I told them, "You better not go anywhere. God knows whom you might encounter. You'd better go upstairs and stay in my son's room until it dawns." And that's how it happened. We locked up the cafe and all of us went upstairs. My wife and I stayed on the first floor which is where we normally live and they were on the second floor where my son normally lives. Naturally, nobody could fall asleep. We sat there drinking coffee, trying to make phone calls. The phones were not working and the shooting spread to the other part of town; however, it wasn't intense. This is how we were when it dawned. The men were upstairs, these guys were upstairs and I went upstairs and as I have already told you from my balcony, one could see quite a lot. The view was good. And at that time, they started shooting at my house from the direction of the health care centre. The balcony was somewhat sheltered. It had an elevated part so it sheltered us and they didn't hit us but some ten bullets hit the door and broke the window pane so I would say that some 30 to 40 bullets had been fired. I managed to get a hold of a broom and since we had a rope for hanging laundry there, I managed to use the broom and to raise a white garment high up in the air and after that, they stopped shooting. We looked out carefully and saw that there was no shooting anymore and then we saw a commotion in front of the health care centre. We saw some seven to eight soldiers there, this is about 150 metres from my house. I don't think it's more than that. We saw soldiers, but they didn't do anything and they didn't head towards our house, but rather went to a side street leading to downtown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the 17th of April, the following day, did you leave your house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere. Since the command was right across the road, I didn't even have to make a phone call, I could just yell out and I saw a soldier on duty there downstairs so I could even speak to him directly. However, regardless of that, I called them on the phone and somebody told me that Radovan, the commander, had gone to Pelagicevo and that he hadn't said anything regarding the activity. So they told me that I'd better stay at home and that's what I did I stayed at home. And then later on, when Radovan came back, I called him up again and he told me: "There is no need for you to come, I'll call you when I need you." These two guys remained there until that afternoon or there about and since there was nothing going on, there were no significant activities, they went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did the phones start working again? When were you able to talk to the command and later with Radovan Antic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Well, I called Radovan in the morning, around 8.00 or 9.00 for the first time, but he already wasn't there, he had already gone to Pelagicevo. The second time I called him was about maybe 11.00. I could see when the car came because this is across the street from me, I could see that the car arrived and that's when I called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what happened after that, what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: The next day, Radovan called me and I went across the street. I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to see him. Since the phones were working, I had already called some other people and I asked them what was going on and the people told me so I knew what had happened. So when I went to see Radovan, he said that the commander of the Tactical Group ordered that a part of the 4th Detachment takes the border areas around the Bosna River and that a part of the 4th Detachment should go about collecting the illegal weapons. It's clear that I didn't have any concrete tasks in this matter because this was done by the units. The commander of the battalion issued orders to the commanders of the companies, then the commanders would go to their companies. They would then issue orders to the section commanders and then the soldiers were then issued with the orders only once the section commander came or if the whole company was lined up. So the commander told me, since the activities of the soldiers had already started, not only in the 4th Detachment but of others, that it would be necessary to see if it would be -- if it is possible to form a kitchen in the Tekstilac, that was this other building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the witness to finish his answer. I'm not objecting to anything, if Your Honours please. I just seek a clarification and I think the Chamber should also have this clarified for them. The witness spoke of -- Mr. Tadic spoke of the commander of the battalion issued orders to the commanders of the companies and the commanders would go to their companies. I take it that the battalion referred to there is in fact the 4th detachment and if I am wrong in that, then perhaps that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: When I was talking about Radovan Antic, I was thinking of the 4th Detachment. At that time, it was still called that and he received orders from the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. Radovan issued orders to his subordinates and they were the commanders of the companies that were also members of the 4th Detachment, and they, in turn, issued orders to their subordinates to soldiers who were members of the 4th Detachment. So I was talking about members of the 4th Detachment only at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification for the transcript, when you mentioned those who were firing at your house, were they soldiers or those people in the camouflage uniforms in the multi-coloured uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: We were able to see those men well. They were the ones in the multi-coloured uniforms, the special forces. Had it been any of the locals, they probably would not have fired at my house because they knew it was my house and would have had no reason to fire at it. But the men in the multi-coloured uniforms were afraid of any house or any corner because they knew that there were armed people in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We had started to talk about the kitchen. Which task were you given, who gave it to you, and what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I've already said somewhere here that I received this task from Commander Radovan Antic and I also said that besides the 4th Detachment, there were other soldiers in Samac and those people needed to be fed so a meal had to be provided for that day. We agreed, we thought about where the best place for that would be and we agreed that it would be the Tekstilac facility because they had a kitchen, that's what we called it at the time, social canteen, the cafeteria, because this facility had a lot of workers there before the war. It employed more than 1.000 people so it had a very large cafeteria and kitchen facilities, a lot of pots and pans and all the other utensils necessary for food preparation. So I took this task upon myself, this was my specific task as a logistics person and Radovan Antic ordered the rest of the 4th Detachment to start collecting the weapons. So the 4th Detachment was not to collect weapons from the whole of the town, but it would only be the neighbourhood marked as the 4th district. So perhaps I will have an opportunity to show you what the 4th district is. This embankment on the River Bosna is also in this 4th district and also a part of the embankment of the River Sava they also belong to the 4th district. It's clear that it was essential to find people who would set up this kitchen and get it going. I went over there and I found this porter and there were also some soldiers who were already doing something in another part of this Tekstilac facility and I asked him -- I never entered this Sit before, so I asked who were the cooks, who is the warehouse person. He explained to me that the warehouse person is this man. He told me who the cooks were, gave me their names, and I tried to find those people. I found some of those women who had worked in the kitchen before. Some women applied who had not been working as cooks before and then this warehouse person opened up the warehouse and food was taken from there. In the beginning it was necessary to have somebody who could manage this kitchen because I wasn't able to do that, so there was a man who was also in the catering business, his name was Djoko Arsenic, I think, and he was in the food service industry. Anyway, he knew those jobs, he was a director of a hotel for a while also. So he took upon himself to manage and to take care of the technical organisational part. He found the food, he issued assignments to the cooks because he knew how to do that better than I did. So this is how this kitchen was set up where the soldiers were fed. Citizens at that time did not have the possibility to cook for themselves, there was no water, there was no electricity so there were a lot of people who regularly came also. It was a very big kitchen and 300 or 400 people at a time could be seated there. So when the soldiers finished their meal, then the citizens would come afterwards and have their meals there. This was the practice later, in particular when it was already very difficult regarding the food situation, so many people did come there to get food.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any other kitchens like that in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: At the same time, at the other end of town, another kitchen also was set up also in a former company, I think the company was called Utva. So on the premises of the Utva company, this restaurant served both Utva and Uniglas, they both used that kitchen. It was completely equipped so it was necessary just to unlock the kitchen and to call the people who worked there before. So this kitchen also was operational and it covered that part of town so that people wouldn't have to walk to 3 kilometres to get to this first kitchen but they could get to the second kitchen for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this period when you were in the kitchen when you were organising this work, and we'll see how long that was, do you know whether food was distributed from that kitchen and if so, where was it distributed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, those soldiers who were at their posts, and we talked about that, so they were on duty at their posts along the River Bosna, the River Sava, at Grebnice, along the line, they were not able to leave the line and go and have lunch, for example. Also, the police, detainees, people who were not able to come to lunch. There was a vehicle with soldiers, army rations, these are special containers for this food, and food can remain quite warm for a long time in these special containers so, for example, one of these containers was enough to feed 20 people. So this vehicle would then go and visit all the posts and distribute food to all of the men who were on those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned detention. Do you have direct knowledge that in that period from the kitchen whose work you organised covered the feeding of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I said that everybody received food from that kitchen, guards, policemen, and also detainees so a food container, for example, would be taken. For example, if there were 20 detainees and 10 police officers, then two of those food containers would be taken and this would be distributed over there. After that, the food containers were collected. So for a certain period, both detainees and soldiers and civilians all ate from the same pot they didn't have different food to eat because it didn't seem economical to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the translation to finish, if Your Honours please. It's not clear to me, and I think it's important for the Chamber to know, is Mr. Tadic saying that food distribution to prisoners took place on the day that he was sent to the kitchens, that is, I think, the 18th or 17th, or is he speaking generally about the following weeks and days? Because the way I understand his evidence is that food was being cooked and given to prisoners immediately and therefore prisoners were in existence immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, just to clarify, you were called by Antic on the 18th. How much time did you need when this kitchen started functioning after the 18th and how long did you participate in the work of this kitchen; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC
utterances.text: I think that the kitchen started to function on the same day, but here I was talking about the way distribution was carried out. So I said that as an example, whether this was on the 18th or the 19th or whether the inmates received food on the 20th. I'm just talking about the way the distribution was organised, but I cannot connect that to a specific date. It was done as needed. So on the 18th, there was nobody, for example, detained so food wasn't taken. If there were ten, then food was provided for ten and the same goes for soldiers. If there were ten of them on the line, it was taken, the food was taken for ten of them, so I'm just only giving examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that it is time to stop, perhaps, with the examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tadic, go and sit in his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber was informed that there were some statements which were ready for submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. According to what I promised yesterday, I have here all the statements translated. These are statements taken during our mission in Bosanski Samac in December and first statement that I would like to tender into evidence is the statement of Witness Djuro Prgomet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: These statements will be numbered for identification purposes only so can you start with the first one. And these statements are for the witnesses of Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can we now have the number? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first statement and the name is -- I can say the name -- Djuro Prgomet, D33/4 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we be given our copies? And the copies in Serbo-Croat will have the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And there is also an English translation after the B/C/S version. They are put together, one after another.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For correction, the English would be D33/4 ID and the B/C/S version is D33/4 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The next statement that we would like to tender into evidence is the statement of Witness Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Next statement that we would like to tender is the statement of Witness Fatima Zaric.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we proceed? The next statement that we would like to tender is statement of Witness Vaso Antic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to inform the Trial Chamber that we have collected two more statements according to Rule 92 bis during our stay in Belgrade and Mr. Pisarevic will bring them in The Hague on Monday, and this is when we are going to give them to be translated and tender them into evidence as soon as we manage with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will now adjourn and continue our proceedings on Monday. Next week, for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, we have the courtroom since the other case is not sitting so in the afternoon we will sit for an extra one and a half hours from 1500 to 1630 hours, that is Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday besides our normal sessions in the morning. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, I suppose you have to sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't wish to take away from your weekend but I was informed by the Registry that we can sit both in the morning and in the afternoon next week. Since my witness has already started testifying, I was unable to approach him regarding that, but prior to the beginning, I asked him in view of his health --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the accused were brought here into the courtroom, just before we began our hearing, I asked him whether we could agree to these new hours to sit both in the morning and in the afternoon and my client just told me very briefly that he would be unable to carry out with that schedule. So could we ask Mr. Tadic now, in view of the pain he has in his leg, a very intense pain at that, could we ask him whether he could agree to sit both in the morning and in the afternoon. Could he address the Chamber himself or could we later inform the Chamber about that, as I was unable to speak to him directly. I worry that this lunch break, which is one and a half hour long could have a negative effect on him. I saw him in prison today. He has trouble walking. He doesn't like to complain about this, but I could see that it was causing him pain and I'm sure that the doctor in the detention unit could affirm this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, but we haven't had a medical report at all. I remember this was said sometime back, but there's no medical report. And one would have thought that it would be advantageous for him so that he would complete his evidence early enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking, Your Honour, as far as I am concerned, I think that would be fine and I think my client would agree with this, but I am afraid that in view of a one and a half hour lunch break, his concentration might slip in the afternoon. This is what he told me that his head -- this intense pain over the past few days and weeks, he underwent therapy and he doesn't have to use crutches anymore, but I could see today that he limps when he walks and we didn't manage to talk about his going to the doctor. We were so busy preparing for his testimony that we had no chance to discuss this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance to the Chamber and to Mr. Lukic, the Prosecution has no objection to Mr. Lukic conferring with his client over that issue, of course, as long as it's confined to that issue if that may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic has just told me that he has to spend six hours here no matter what and he feels very bad about that both in view of his age and his problems with prostate and his osteoporosis and other ailments including this one with his leg so it is very difficult for him to sit for longer than the half a day session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I did say that you should have got a medical report for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do that on Monday, as early as Monday. You did tell us that we should look out for any changes, but the initial courtroom schedule envisaged us working only half a day, and therefore, I was unable to contact my client and see how he felt about this. I think if the Registry assists us, we should be able to obtain a medical report as early as Monday afternoon in which a doctor could tell us whether my client is able to spend here the entire day. As far as we are concerned, we are prepared to complete his testimony as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will sit those hours on Monday and see how it will go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
